description_full: Anterix Inc. operates as holder of licensed 900 MHz spectrum with coverage spanning the contiguous to utility and critical infrastructure enterprise customers in the United States, Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico. It offers TowerX, a tower site access services; CatalyX, a turnkey connectivity management solution; and Anterix Active Ecosystem. The company was formerly known as pdvWireless, Inc. and changed its name to Anterix Inc. in August 2019. Anterix Inc. was incorporated in 1997 and is based in Woodland Park, New Jersey.

financial_summary: Anterix Inc. is a small-cap communication services business with a $1.6B market cap on $7M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +50% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +171.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at -11% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and -12% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $5M in free cash flow — roughly 84 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.06×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +18.3% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin -10575.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.1%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 177% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 70.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
